Section 1 of 14

What if the thing that once helped you escape is now controlling your life?

Addiction often begins with the desire to feel different.

Someone may want relief from pain, trauma, loneliness, stress, anger, or memories that will not stay quiet. A substance or behavior may offer a few moments of escape. But over time, what promised relief can become another kind of prison.

You may tell yourself:

“I can stop whenever I want.”
“This will be the last time.”
“No one knows how bad it has become.”
“I have already failed too many times.”

Jesus does not look at you and see a hopeless person. He sees someone worth rescuing.

Addiction can involve physical dependence, changes in the brain, learned behavior, emotional wounds, relationships, environment, and spiritual bondage. It is not overcome by shame. Recovery usually requires truth, surrender, treatment, supportive people, and daily choices.

The chains may be strong, but Jesus is stronger.

Addiction is not a Native identity

Native people have sometimes been unfairly stereotyped as though addiction belongs to Native cultures.

It does not.

Addiction affects people of every nation, income, age, and background. Native communities also carry distinct histories. Forced displacement, family separation, boarding schools, abuse, poverty, and other forms of trauma have caused real wounds.

Pain can increase a person’s vulnerability to harmful coping, but pain does not determine anyone’s future. Native identity should be connected with dignity, endurance, family, community, and survival—not reduced to a stereotype about substances.

Your struggle is something you are facing. It is not who you are.

When does something become an addiction?

Read 2 Peter 2:19 ↗.

The Bible says:

“A person is a slave to whatever has mastered him.”

A substance or behavior may be gaining control if you:

  • Use more than you intended
  • Repeatedly try to stop but cannot
  • Hide or lie about it
  • Need more to experience the same effect
  • Feel sick, anxious, or unstable without it
  • Continue despite damage to health or relationships
  • Neglect work, school, family, or responsibilities
  • Spend money needed for basic needs
  • Take dangerous risks while using
  • Think about it throughout the day
  • Use it mainly to escape emotional pain

Addiction is recognized as a treatable health disorder involving lasting changes in reward, stress, and self-control systems. That does not remove personal responsibility, but it explains why sincere promises alone may not be enough. The National Institute on Drug Abuse explains how addiction affects behavior and the brain. ↗

You may need spiritual help and professional treatment. Receiving both is not a contradiction.

What can become controlling?

People may become dependent on:

  • Alcohol
  • Opioids or other drugs
  • Misused prescription medication
  • Methamphetamine, cocaine, or other stimulants
  • Commercial tobacco and nicotine
  • Marijuana or other intoxicating substances
  • Gambling
  • Pornography
  • Compulsive sexual behavior
  • Gaming or social media
  • Shopping
  • Food-related behaviors

Not every repeated behavior is an addiction. But anything that controls your choices, harms your life, and repeatedly defeats your desire to stop should be taken seriously.

Your body belongs to the Creator

Read 1 Corinthians 6:19–20 ↗.

Your body is described as a temple of the Holy Spirit. It was created by God and purchased at an immeasurable cost through Jesus.

This does not mean you should hate your body when you struggle. It means your body is worth protecting.

The Creator wants freedom for your mind as well as your body. Read 1 Peter 5:8 ↗. He calls us to be sober and alert because clear thinking helps us recognize temptation and make wise choices.

The safest path is to avoid alcohol, commercial tobacco, recreational intoxicants, and the misuse of medication. A prescription should be used only as directed by a qualified health professional.

Alcohol promises relief but takes control

Read Proverbs 20:1 ↗ and Proverbs 23:29–35 ↗.

The Bible describes alcohol’s ability to distort judgment, increase conflict, cause injury, and create a desire for more.

Alcohol can numb pain temporarily, but it cannot heal the wound beneath it. When the effect wears off, the pain remains—and may be joined by regret, damaged relationships, financial problems, or dependence.

Read Ephesians 5:18 ↗.

The Bible contrasts being controlled by alcohol with being filled by the Holy Spirit. The Creator wants your mind available to Him rather than controlled by a substance.

Respect the difference between traditional and commercial tobacco

Some Native nations have traditional uses of tobacco. Those practices vary greatly, and they should not be confused with commercial tobacco products manufactured and sold for profit.

The CDC distinguishes traditional tobacco from commercial cigarettes, chewing tobacco, and similar products. It notes that traditional tobacco varies among nations and is often not inhaled, while commercial tobacco contains harmful chemicals and is sold in ways that create dependence. Read the CDC’s explanation of this important distinction. ↗

Recognizing that distinction does not decide whether every spiritual use agrees with the Bible. As discussed in Lesson 19, each practice should be understood accurately and then examined by Scripture.

This lesson’s health concern is clear: nicotine dependence and exposure to harmful smoke can damage the body. Commercial tobacco should not be allowed to claim control over a life that belongs to the Creator.

Jesus came to set captives free

Read Luke 4:16–21 ↗ and John 8:34–36 ↗.

Jesus announced freedom for captives. He was speaking about more than physical prison. Sin itself becomes a form of slavery.

Jesus said:

“If the Son makes you free, you shall be free indeed.”

Freedom may happen suddenly for some people. They pray, surrender the addiction, and never return to it.

For others, freedom develops through treatment, accountability, repeated choices, and learning how to face pain without escaping through a substance.

Both kinds of recovery require the power and grace of Jesus.

Do not compare your path with someone else’s testimony. A longer recovery does not mean Jesus has abandoned you.

Begin by telling the truth

Read Psalm 32:3–5 ↗.

Secrecy gives addiction room to grow. Recovery begins when you stop protecting what is hurting you.

Tell the Creator the truth:

“I am not in control.”
“I need help.”
“I have hurt people.”
“I am afraid to stop.”
“I do not know how to live without this.”

Then tell one trustworthy person. Choose someone who can respond with wisdom, confidentiality, and practical help—a qualified counselor, physician, recovery professional, mature spiritual leader, or reliable family member.

Confession is not meant to humiliate you. It brings the struggle into the light.

Do not face dangerous withdrawal alone

Stopping certain substances suddenly can be medically dangerous.

If you drink heavily or regularly, alcohol withdrawal can become life-threatening. Speak with a medical professional before trying to detox alone. The National Institute on Alcohol Abuse and Alcoholism explains the need for medical assessment and support. ↗

Benzodiazepine medications—such as certain medicines prescribed for anxiety, panic, or sleep—can also cause dangerous withdrawal if stopped suddenly or reduced too quickly. Work with a qualified prescriber on a safe plan. The FDA warns that abrupt withdrawal can cause life-threatening reactions. ↗

Prayer is essential, but prayer does not turn a dangerous detox into a safe one. The Creator can work through doctors, treatment centers, medication, counselors, and recovery programs.

Seeking medical help is not weak faith. It is wise stewardship of your life.

Treatment can be part of the Creator’s answer

Some people have been told that if they really trusted Jesus, they would not need counseling or medication.

That claim is harmful.

The Creator heals in different ways. Sometimes healing is immediate. Sometimes He works through trained people and a carefully planned process.

Treatment may include:

  • Medical evaluation
  • Supervised withdrawal management
  • Individual counseling
  • Group treatment
  • Residential or outpatient programs
  • Trauma-informed care
  • Medication
  • Peer recovery groups
  • Family counseling
  • Long-term follow-up

For opioid use disorder, medicines such as buprenorphine and methadone can reduce opioid use and help people remain in treatment. Medication is not proof that someone has failed spiritually. Current medical guidance recognizes these treatments as effective and lifesaving. ↗

Look for care that respects your dignity, faith, family relationships, and cultural identity. The Indian Health Service treatment locator ↗ can help locate IHS, Tribal, and Urban Indian health programs.

Build a practical freedom plan

  1. Identify what controls you

Name the substance or behavior clearly. Write down what it has cost you physically, spiritually, financially, and relationally.

  1. Identify your triggers

Notice the people, places, emotions, times, and situations connected with use.

Common triggers include:

  • Conflict
  • Loneliness
  • Paydays
  • Certain friends
  • Trauma memories
  • Boredom
  • Shame
  • Celebrations
  • Lack of sleep
  • Social media content

Knowing a trigger allows you to plan before it arrives.

  1. Remove access

Dispose of substances safely. Delete contacts connected with obtaining them. Block gambling or pornography sites. Avoid locations where relapse is likely.

Do not keep temptation close merely to prove you are strong.

  1. Replace the old routine

Removing an addiction leaves an empty space. Fill it intentionally.

Healthy replacements may include exercise, sleep, prayer, time outside, cooking, music, service, counseling, learning a skill, and safe time with supportive people.

  1. Contact someone before giving in

Choose two or three people you can call when cravings become strong. Do not wait until after the decision has been made.

A simple message can say:

“I am struggling right now. Can you stay with me or talk for a few minutes?”
  1. Protect your daily spiritual life

Read the Bible, pray, and ask for the Holy Spirit every day. Memorize promises you can repeat when temptation comes.

Read 1 Corinthians 10:13 ↗.

The Creator promises to provide a way of escape. The escape may be leaving a room, calling someone, surrendering your phone, attending a meeting, entering treatment, or asking for immediate help.

When the escape appears, take it.

Healing may require facing the pain beneath the addiction

Read Psalm 34:18 ↗.

The Creator is close to people with broken hearts.

Substances and compulsive behaviors often become ways to avoid grief, trauma, rejection, anger, or shame. Removing the addiction without addressing the pain can leave a person vulnerable to relapse or to replacing one addiction with another.

A qualified counselor can help you face painful experiences safely. A trustworthy spiritual community can provide prayer, connection, and support.

You do not have to describe traumatic experiences publicly to prove you want healing. You control when, where, and with whom you share your story.

Your pain deserves careful, respectful attention.

What if you relapse?

Relapse does not mean recovery is impossible or that all previous progress was fake.

It means your plan needs immediate attention. Contact your treatment provider and support person. Identify what led to the relapse, strengthen the plan, and continue.

Do not allow shame to turn one harmful choice into a long return to addiction.

Relapse can also be physically dangerous. After a period without a drug, the body may lose tolerance. Returning to a previous dose can cause an overdose. Medical guidance warns that relapse may require resumed or adjusted treatment and immediate safety planning. ↗

Jesus does not tell you to stay on the ground because you fell.

Read Micah 7:8 ↗.

Rise again and reach for help.

Helping someone you love

You cannot force another person into lasting recovery, but you can respond with truth and love.

You can:

  • Speak when the person is sober
  • Describe specific behavior instead of attacking character
  • Encourage professional treatment
  • Offer transportation to an appointment
  • Refuse to provide money that supports the addiction
  • Protect children and vulnerable people
  • Maintain clear boundaries
  • Keep emergency help available
  • Seek support for yourself

Love does not mean covering up dangerous behavior. Forgiveness does not mean removing every consequence.

If someone becomes violent or threatens you, move to safety and contact emergency help. You are not required to remain in danger to prove your love.

Know what to do during an opioid overdose

Signs can include inability to awaken, slow or stopped breathing, choking or gurgling sounds, discolored lips or nails, and very small pupils.

If you suspect an opioid overdose, treat it as an emergency:

  1. Give naloxone if it is available.
  2. Call 911 immediately.
  3. Try to keep the person breathing.
  4. Place the person on their side to reduce choking risk.
  5. Stay until emergency help arrives.

Naloxone can temporarily reverse an opioid overdose, but emergency care is still necessary. The CDC provides complete overdose-response instructions. ↗

Carrying naloxone does not encourage drug use. It gives someone another chance to live and choose recovery.

You can ask for help today

In the United States:

  • Call 911 if someone is in immediate danger or experiencing an overdose.
  • Call or text 988 for immediate support during a suicidal or emotional crisis. The 988 Lifeline ↗ is available around the clock.
  • Call SAMHSA’s National Helpline at 1-800-662-HELP (4357) for free, confidential treatment information.
  • Visit FindTreatment.gov ↗ to search for substance-use and mental-health treatment.
  • Use the IHS Treatment Locator ↗ to search for IHS, Tribal, or Urban Indian health services.

If you are outside the United States, contact your local emergency number or national crisis service.

Asking for help today may be the first act of freedom.

Think About It

  1. Is there a substance or behavior that has gained more control than you want to admit?
  2. What pain, emotion, or situation usually triggers the urge to escape?
  3. Who is one safe person you could tell the truth?
  4. Do you need a medical evaluation before trying to stop?
  5. What people, contacts, apps, objects, or locations should be removed from your life?
  6. What healthy practice could begin filling the space the addiction occupied?

Try This During the Coming Week

Day 1

Read John 8:31–36 ↗.

Write down what freedom through Jesus would look like in your daily life.

Day 2

Read Psalm 32:1–5 ↗.

Tell the Creator the complete truth about your struggle. Then contact one trustworthy person.

Day 3

Read 1 Corinthians 6:19–20 ↗.

Choose one action that will protect your body today.

Day 4

Read 1 Corinthians 10:13 ↗.

Write a plan for what you will do when your strongest trigger appears.

Day 5

Read Psalm 34:17–18 ↗.

Ask what pain may be hiding beneath the addiction. Consider scheduling an appointment with a qualified counselor or treatment provider.

Day 6

Read Romans 6:11–14 ↗.

Remove at least one source of access and replace one unhealthy routine with a healthy one.

Day 7

Read Philippians 2:12–13 ↗.

Review your week without hiding or shaming yourself. Thank the Creator for every step forward and strengthen the parts of your plan that need more support.

A Prayer You Can Pray

Creator, You know what has gained control in my life. You know the pain I have tried to escape and the promises I have made and broken.

I cannot free myself by willpower alone. I need Your help.

Jesus, thank You for seeing me as someone worth rescuing. Forgive me for the harm my choices have caused. Break the spiritual chains that hold me and give me courage to accept practical help.

Holy Spirit, guide me toward safe treatment and trustworthy people. Help me tell the truth, remove access, face my pain, and choose the way of escape when temptation comes.

Protect me from shame when I struggle. If I fall, help me rise quickly and return to You.

My body, mind, and future belong to You. Lead me one day and one decision at a time into real freedom. Amen.

Remember This

Addiction is not your identity, and it is not a Native identity.

It is a serious but treatable condition that can involve physical, emotional, relational, and spiritual bondage.

Jesus offers freedom, but seeking His help does not exclude medical care, counseling, medication, or recovery support. These may be part of His answer.

Do not attempt a dangerous withdrawal alone. Tell the truth, seek qualified help, build a support system, remove access, and keep returning to Jesus.

The chains may be strong, but they do not have to decide the rest of your story.
